name: Zsh
title: Zsh (5.9)
lifecycleNote: 5.9 is still the current stable series

type.text: **Values are strings with no static check**: A scalar, an array element, and an associative-array value all hold text, and no declaration states what kind of thing a name holds
**No sum types**: An alternative is a word plus a convention, and `typeset -A` gives a mapping rather than a tagged choice
**No generics and no dispatch by type**: A routine is specialised only by its positional arguments, and behaviour is selected by the command name (T5, T9)
**One flat namespace**: Functions and parameters share the global space, and `local` only narrows a name inside a function body, so nothing hides a library's internals from the process (T6, T11)
**An unset name expands to nothing by default**: `setopt nounset` turns the reference into an error, but the option is off unless it is requested, and an empty value still passes
**`typeset -T` ties two parameters together**: `typeset -T PATH path` makes the scalar `PATH` and the array `path` one value in two shapes, so colon-separated data is edited as a list

construction.text: **Global by default and mutable by default**: An assignment writes the global unless `local` or `typeset` narrows it, and no binding is immutable unless `readonly` is applied (C1, C2)
**No constructor or validation on a plain parameter**: Nothing checks a value when it is bound; validation exists only where `setopt` or an explicit test is applied
**`local` in a function body is a real scope**: A parameter declared local is restored when the function returns, so working state stays with the routine
**`autoload -Uz` separates definition from call**: A function body is loaded from `$fpath` on first reference, so the name is declared without the implementation being read
**Configuration files are layered and sourced by role**: `.zshenv`, `.zprofile`, `.zshrc`, `.zlogin`, and `.zlogout` each hold one kind of setup, so interactive configuration does not reach a script
**`emulate -L zsh` fixes the option set inside a function**: The options are reset for the function's duration and restored on return, so a routine does not inherit settings from the caller

memory.text: **No allocation or free in the language**: There is no pointer and no deallocation builtin; parameters are allocated and released by the shell
**Scope and `unset` bound a lifetime**: A `local` parameter disappears when its function returns, so working state does not persist by accident
**Associative arrays are managed by the shell**: `typeset -A` allocates and grows its own storage, so no capacity handling is written
**Assignment copies the value**: An array is duplicated on assignment, and referencing one without copying requires an explicit indirection
**Command substitution is materialised whole**: `$(cmd)` collects the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so a large result is held in memory
**`always` blocks hold their state until the block ends**: The try and always blocks are kept for the duration of the construct, so a long-running trap delays release

error.text: **No structured error path**: `$?`, `TRAPZERR`, and the `always` block are the apparatus, with no exception and no error value
**The error trap is global and undifferentiated**: `TRAPZERR` runs for the whole script, it receives no description of the failure, and it fires only where a non-zero status is not consumed
**Errors cannot be returned**: A function's outcome is an exit status, so an error carries no payload and cannot be combined with another
**`{ ... } always { ... }` guarantees cleanup**: The always block runs after an error, a `break`, or a `continue`, so teardown is attached to the construct rather than to a global trap
**The always block does not survive a parse error**: A syntax error in the try list aborts during parsing, so the always list never runs
**`setopt errexit` is fragile**: The option does not fire inside `&&` and `||` chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes error behaviour

concurrency.text: **No concurrency primitives**: There is no lock, channel, mutex, or await; the only parallel construct is a background job

**`zmodload zsh/system` adds real synchronisation**: The module provides a `zsystem` builtin with file locking and a `sysread`/`syswrite` pair, so a race over a shared file can be avoided in the language
**Processes are the unit of parallelism**: Concurrency is expressed with pipes and background jobs, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
**Coprocesses give two-way communication**: `coproc` starts a child that `print -p` and `read -p` can drive, so a long-running program is not restarted per iteration
**Background jobs inherit the environment**: A `&` job shares every global parameter, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
**`wait` returns a status, not a value**: A result must travel through a file, a pipe, or a coprocess

platform.text: **One implementation defines the language**: Zsh exists as the zsh project's own C implementation, with no independent implementation of the same specification to compare against
**zsh is packaged for every UNIX-like system**: Linux distributions, the BSDs, and macOS all ship it, and it is the default interactive shell on macOS
**The implementation runs on POSIX systems and Windows**: The same code base builds on Linux, the BSDs, Solaris, and through Cygwin or MSYS2 on Windows

**`emulate sh` is a compatibility mode, not POSIX compliance**: The shell can be invoked as `sh` or `ksh` and behave closer to them, but the mode is offered for convenience rather than as a conformance claim
**Open-source governance is project-led**: The language is directed by its maintainers in a public repository, with no standards body and no formal change process
**No second implementation is likely**: With a very large option and module surface, an independent implementation would be a research project

performance.text: **Interpreted with no compilation**: Each command is parsed and executed as text, and there is no artifact and no JIT
**A native implementation with a fast path for common work**: Expansion, globbing, and arithmetic are executed in C rather than by calling an external command
**Floating-point arithmetic is built in**: `(( ... ))` handles real numbers, so a numeric calculation does not need `awk` or `bc`
**`zmodload zsh/mathfunc` adds the C math library**: Trigonometric and logarithmic functions are available inside arithmetic expressions

**Start-up sources several configuration files**: An interactive shell reads `.zshenv`, then `.zprofile` or `.zshrc`, so a large `oh-my-zsh` setup costs time on every new shell, which `zsh/zprof` can measure
**The completion system builds a cache**: `compinit` scans `$fpath` and writes `~/.zcompdump`, so the first shell after a change pays for the scan

ecosystem.text: **No package manager in the language**: There is no dependency resolver, so plugins arrive through third-party frameworks such as `oh-my-zsh`, `prezto`, `zinit`, or `antigen`
**The plugin ecosystem is one of the largest in the shell world**: Prompt themes, completions, and syntax-highlighting plugins exist for most command-line tools
**The bundled completion system is extensive**: `_arguments` definitions ship for hundreds of commands, and `compinit` makes them all available without an add-on
**`vcs_info` provides a git-aware prompt in the standard distribution**: Version-control state is read by a shipped module instead of a script
**Documentation is complete and versioned**: The manual is shipped as man pages and as a searchable HTML manual
**Frameworks own the configuration**: `oh-my-zsh` and its alternatives take over `.zshrc`, so a user's setup depends on a third-party project

evolution.text: **No breaking-change culture**: New releases add features, and the project documents the few changes that affect existing configuration
**`emulate` pins behaviour**: A script can fix the option set with `emulate -L zsh`, so a change of defaults does not silently alter it
**The project ships regular releases**: The 5.x series has been maintained for many years with ongoing fixes
**Options are the compatibility mechanism**: A new behaviour is normally introduced behind a `setopt`, so the old behaviour remains available
**Change depends on the maintainers**: The language is directed by its project team rather than by a committee with a published process
**Frameworks must track the language**: A plugin that depends on internal behaviour can break when a release changes it, which is a risk of the ecosystem rather than of the language

domain.text: **Excellent for interactive use**: The completion system, prompt substitution, and `vcs_info` make the terminal the primary domain
**Strong for text and path processing**: Glob qualifiers such as `*(.)` for plain files, recursive `**/`, and `setopt extendedglob` express selection that other shells delegate to `find`
**Arrays and associative arrays fit scripting that needs structure**: `typeset -A` and array slicing cover indexed and keyed data inside the language
**Emulation covers other shells when needed**: `emulate sh` and `emulate ksh` run foreign syntax in a nested scope
**A zsh script needs zsh**: An interpreter that is not installed on every host, so a portable bootstrap script cannot be written in zsh
**The most useful features are interactive**: Completion, prompt themes, and autosuggestions do not travel into a script

learning.text: **Bash knowledge transfers**: The core syntax, expansions, and pipelines are familiar to a Bash user
**Documentation is complete and searchable**: The manual covers the language, the builtins, the options, and the modules
**Parameter expansion is more complex than in Bash**: `${(flags)name}` and the `setopt`-controlled variations each have their own rule
**The option set is very large**: The behaviour of a script depends on which options are set, and a reader must know the current set
**Framework configuration hides the setup**: An `oh-my-zsh` user learns the framework before the language

syntax.text: **Arrays are first-class with slicing**: `$a[2,-1]` expresses a range that other shells express with a loop
**Glob qualifiers replace external tools**: `*(.)`, `*(/D)`, and `**/*.c` select files by kind and recursion in the pattern itself
**No word splitting by default**: An unquoted `$var` expands as one word even when it contains spaces, so fewer quotes are needed
**Parameter expansion flags are dense**: `${(q)var}`, `${(j:,:)a}`, and `${(k)assoc}` pack quoting, joining, and keys into a short notation
**`setopt` changes the reading of the text**: The same script behaves differently under `shwordsplit`, `nomatch`, or `extendedglob`
**Arrays may be 0-indexed or 1-indexed**: The default is 1-indexed while `KSH_ARRAYS` changes it, so an array index is not always portable between zsh configurations

testing.text: **No test framework in the language**: A test is a script that checks `$?`, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility
**Faults appear only on the branch that runs**: With no static check, a mistyped parameter or a bad array index is found during the run
**A syntax check runs without execution**: `zsh -n` parses a script and reports errors without running it
**`functions -T` traces a selected function**: Tracing can be limited to the function under test instead of the whole script
**`TRAPDEBUG` gives a debugger hook**: A function bound to the DEBUG trap runs before each command, which supports a stepping harness
**The test set can be isolated with `emulate -L zsh` and a subshell**: Each case runs with known options in a child process

security.text: **Dynamic typing removes a check the shell cannot make**: A value that should be a path, a number, or a flag is a string, and only the command that receives it can object
**Text can re-enter the interpreter**: A value assembled from data and passed to `eval`, or interpolated into a substituted command, becomes code
**`nomatch` controls a failure mode rather than removing it**: An unmatched glob either errors or expands literally, so the script must choose which surprise it prefers
**`setopt nounset` turns an unset reference into an error**: A misspelled parameter is reported instead of expanding to nothing
**`${(q)var}` quotes a value for re-input**: The expansion flag makes safe quoting explicit instead of leaving it to hand-written escaping
**`setopt noclobber` protects existing files**: The option makes `>` refuse to overwrite a regular file

tradeoffs: **The large option set is a deliberate design**: `setopt` lets a user choose behaviour that other shells fix, and the price is that a script must state which behaviour it expects
**The completion system is a language of its own**: `compinit`, `_arguments`, and `zstyle` make completion programmable, which is a feature rather than a coupling mechanism
**Modules are optional capability**: `zmodload` adds `zsh/mathfunc`, `zsh/datetime`, and `zsh/system` on demand, so a script chooses its own surface
**1-indexed arrays were a compatibility decision**: The offset differs from Bash and ksh, and `KSH_ARRAYS` exists for users who want the other convention
**`oh-my-zsh` is a distribution, not the language**: The framework owns configuration and the prompt, so its coupling is to the user's setup rather than to zsh itself
**zsh is not a general-purpose language**: The model is a shell over external commands, which is a scope decision
verdict: Zsh keeps the core coupling of a word-based shell — one namespace, no static typing, and an exit status in place of an error value — so its core score stays low, but it removes real friction inside that model: `typeset -T` ties `PATH` to the `path` array, `{ ... } always { ... }` guarantees cleanup, `autoload -Uz` separates a name from its body, and glob qualifiers express selection that other shells leave to `find`. The ecosystem score reflects the strongest interactive tooling in the family: a large bundled completion system, shipped modules such as `vcs_info` and `zsh/system`, and documentation that keeps pace with the releases. The remaining cost is that zsh is one implementation, its option set is large, and a framework usually owns the configuration.

energy.text: Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The installed interpreter reads the source at run time; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
